neutral_facts.value: The accused, a man, assaulted his wife with a chopper on her neck in their bedroom, resulting in her death. The victim's body was discovered by neighbors, covered in blood. The accused was seen by witnesses carrying a blood-stained chopper and his 8-month-old son. The medical examination of the victim's body confirmed injuries consistent with the weapon seized from the accused. The accused claimed insanity due to paranoid schizophrenia, but the courts found no evidence he was mentally ill at the time of the crime. The accused had a history of treatment for a psychotic disorder in 1985, but there was no indication of mental illness post-1985. The accused's actions, including leaving the child with a neighbor and confessing to the crime, suggested he understood the nature of his actions.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant assaulted his wife with a chopper on her neck, resulting in her death. The evidence, including ocular and medical testimony, corroborated the act, and the appellant's conduct before and after the incident indicated his awareness of the nature of his actions.

quotes.text: The prosecution version as it emerges through the evidence of PW1 and PW5. It was alleged that on 3.11.2000 at about 7.30 p.m. The appellant with the intention of killing his wife, namely, Ajitha @ Poonamma had struck her on her neck with a chopper when she was in the bedroom of his house which is named 'Kallumkuzhi', bearing No.289 situated in ward No. IX of Kanjikuzhy panchayat.

defence_argument.value: The defence claimed the appellant suffered from paranoid schizophrenia and that his cognitive faculties were impaired at the time of the crime, making him incapable of knowing the nature of his act. They argued that the medical evidence supported this claim.

quotes.text: The plea taken in the instant case was also that the appellant was suffering from 'paranoid schizophrenia'. The medical profession would undoubtedly treat the appellant as a mentally sick person. However, for the purposes of claiming the benefit of the defence of insanity in law, the appellant would have to prove that his cognitive faculties were so impaired, at the time when the crime was committed, as not to know the nature of the act.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the accused must prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that at the time of the crime, he was incapable of knowing the nature of his act or that it was wrong or contrary to law, as per Section 84 of the Indian Penal Code.

quotes.text: Section 84 IPC clearly gives statutory recognition to the defence of insanity. A bare perusal of the Section 84 would show that in order to succeed, the appellant would have to prove that by reason of unsoundness of mind, he was incapable of knowing the nature of the act committed by him.

sentencing_rationale.value: The final sentence was imposed because the courts concluded that the appellant was fully aware of the nature of his act and its consequences, and there was no evidence to support his claim of insanity at the time of the crime.

quotes.text: The conduct of the appellant before and after the incident was sufficient to negate any notion that he was mentally insane, so as not to be possessed of the necessary mens rea, for committing the murder of his wife.
